facets.title: Facet 2: Wellness amenities footprint (pools, hot tubs, saunas, spa/massage, gyms, towel laundry)

nodes.t: CIBSE TM46:2008 benchmarks: swimming pool centre 245 elec + 1,130 fossil kWh/m2 floor/yr; fitness & health centre 160 + 440; hotel 105 + 330
Kampel 2016 (via Smedegård 2021): Norwegian swimming facilities EPI mean 26, median ~22, range 10–80 kWh/visitor; specific energy 400–1,600 kWh/m2·a; 28% excess
Nitter et al. NTNU survey (2017 data): Norwegian pool facilities 6.7–35 kWh/bather climate-corrected; bathers + opening days explain 77%; ACH 2.65 (water parks) vs 4.81 (conventional)

Trianti-Stourna 1998 (Greek pools, secondhand): 450 kWh/m2 floor, 1,094.5 kWh/m2 water surface, 57.5 kWh/m2 electricity — but also quoted as 4,300 (Mediterranean) / 5,200 (continental) kWh/m2 water surface; inconsistent
Borowski et al. 2022 (Kraków hotel, metered): pool-area heating 399.6–657.4 kWh/day (June–May), peak 63.7 kWh/h; hotel 4,620 m2, 51 rooms
Evaporation is the dominant pool heat loss: 46–54% of total pool losses (Thermal Science 2014 simulation); "at least 60% of heat loss in the water" (Benakcha 2025 collating 4 studies)
Sport England 2013 pool design conditions: water 27–30°C (hydrotherapy 35, spa pools 40), hall air ~30°C (1°C above water), RH 60±10%, 4–10 ACH, make-up 30 L/swimmer
Darlington (UK) sports centre with pool + sauna + dry sports, measured: 1,220 kWh/m2/yr total, 480 kWh/m2/yr technical equipment; remainder mostly lighting
ENERGY STAR 2024 US median site EUI: Recreation group (incl. Fitness Center/Health Club/Gym, pools, rinks) 50.8 kBtu/ft2 = 160 kWh/m2/yr; Hotel 63.0 kBtu/ft2 = 199 kWh/m2/yr
ENERGY STAR hotel score model (CBECS 2012, Aug 2018) has no pool/spa/gym term; laundry, occupancy and conference space were tested and found not statistically significant

Hotel EUI regressions without amenity terms: Chan 2005 (17 HK hotels) 313 kWh/m2/yr, only CDD and occupied rooms significant; Wang 2012 (Taiwan) area/rooms/occupancy/age, adj R2 0.928 total, 0.612 EUI; Wang & Huang 2013: 83–408 MJ/guest-night
Santiago 2021 (six Gran Canaria hotels): pool volume is a significant explanatory variable of total hotel energy among 31 characteristics; F&B >50% of energy, DHW next
TRSA 2018 (132 US laundry plants): 1.47 gal/lb water = 12.3 L/kg; 2,422 Btu/lb in-plant energy = 1.57 kWh/kg; 0.413 lb CO2/lb = 0.41 kg CO2/kg; hotel/lodging only 1.2% of pounds

Laundry water/energy per kg: Bobák 2010 professional 5–6 L/kg vs home >20 L/kg, wash-heat 0.21–0.875 kWh/kg (theoretical); UK trade 1.6–1.7 kWh/kg typical, 0.8–1.0 attainable; on-site hotel machines 15–30 L/kg vs 3 L/kg central
Euro Chlor eco-profile (2011 data, pub. 2013), cradle-to-gate GWP: 0.90 kg CO2e/kg chlorine, 0.93 kg CO2e/kg sodium hypochlorite, 0.86 NaOH, 0.06 NaCl
Pool make-up water standard 30 L/bather (Sport England; PWTAG incl. backwash; WHO via Nova Scotia; DIN 19643); Polish measurement 40.6 L/bather/day; one sand-filter backwash ~16 m3 (38 L/s × 7 min)

Hot tubs: only residential data — NSPI 2000 average 2,514 kWh/yr; CA-compliant 334-gal spa ~200 W standby ≈ 1,900 kWh/yr; French 2023 study 2,500–7,500 kWh/yr; heater 6 kW (240 V), pump 1.5 kW; no commercial hotel whirlpool measurement found

Sauna/steam loads (manufacturer nameplates only): Harvia Club 10/12.5/15 kW and Virta Pro HL200E 20 kW; Tylo Commercial 20 kW; Mr Steam CU750 18 kW (CU series 'for continuous or near continuous use', up to 750 ft3); Harvia guidance full power 30-40 min then ~50%; Cleopatra 11.4 kW steam generator at 16 h/day = 66,393 kWh/yr nameplate, ~36,516 at 55% duty. No manufacturer or audit publishes a measured commercial duty cycle; no hotel spa sub-metered sauna/steam/whirlpool study found

Gym equipment loads are small: metered 2 HP treadmill 712 W at 10 mph, 96 W at 1 mph, 3.76 W idle; Horizon plans 1,200–1,800 W; SportsArt ECO-POWR max 200–250 Wh per machine-hour, Bloomberg test 24 W over 30 min

No spa treatment-room energy benchmark exists; only "up to 35% of hotel energy for additional services such as a spa" (Spanish hotels, unsourced) and PwC cost share 4% (basic) vs 25% (spa + heated pools) of hotel management costs

Towel mass from Standard Textile catalogue weights (lb per dozen): hospitality bath towel 27x54 in 15-17 lb/dz = 570-640 g; 25x54 13.5 lb/dz = 510 g; 24x50 10.5 lb/dz = 400 g; hand towel 16x27/16x30 3-4.5 lb/dz = 115-170 g; washcloth 1-1.5 lb/dz = 40-55 g; bath mat 20x30 7 lb/dz = 265 g, 20x34 10.5 lb/dz = 400 g. A spa/pool visit issuing 2 bath + 1 hand towel weighs about 1.3-1.5 kg dry

Hotel laundry mass per occupied room-night: industry range 8-55 lb (3.6-25 kg) PPOR, ~10 PPOR on group-heavy days and ~17 PPOR on high-turnover days, 83 PPOR peak at a 400-room 5-diamond resort (Western State Design, 2017); 12 lb (5.4 kg)/room/day cited for a full-service hotel with pool and banquets; TRSA 44-property benchmark (clean lb per occupied room) is members-only

Only metered hotel-spa electricity benchmark found: Novotel Bali Ngurah Rai Airport spa, Jan-Jun 2024 audit (Politeknik Negeri Bali thesis, I Gde Bagus Arya Putra): 7.24-11.22 kWh/m2/month (87-135 kWh/m2/yr) covering lighting, air conditioning and equipment; AC found oversized in several rooms; no kWh per treatment published

Kampel, Aas & Bruland 2013 (Norwegian swimming halls): delivered energy about 1,000 to nearly 11,000 kWh/m2 water surface per year across facilities; literature comparators 4,300/5,200 (Trianti-Stourna), 5,984 (German spa), 4,475 (Finland) kWh/m2 WS; 725/1,573 kWh/m2 floor UK good/typical practice

Attribute amenities via regression marginal effect on whole-hotel EUI

Attribute amenities bottom-up: sub-metered loads (Kraków 400–660 kWh/day pool heating) plus engineering build-up from design conditions, evaporation physics, nameplate duty cycles and per-kg laundry factors
Bottom-up sub-metered/engineering attribution beats per-m2 water-surface benchmarks and regression marginal effects for wellness amenities

Trianti-Stourna 1998 resolved: 4,300/5,200 kWh/m2 water surface are unsourced climate-zone literature values; the five audited Greek pools averaged 450.1 kWh/m2 usable area (Kampel 2013/2016)

facets.name: Food & beverage
facets.title: Facet 3: Food and beverage footprint (restaurants, bars, buffets, room service, banquets, minibars, food waste)

nodes.t: Dolder Grand 2023-25: F&B = 48/52/56% of whole-hotel CO2e; 5.4-6.1 kgCO2e per restaurant guest; 38-39 kg per overnight stay
Accor URD 2024: catering & drinks 19% (1,229 kt) vs energy 65% of group footprint; 1.66-6.57 kgCO2e per meal (2023)
SHA 2024: hotel food systems 185 MtCO2e/yr; sourcing 62%, kitchen energy 19%, food waste 17%, packaging 2%; hotel meal ~3x global-average meal
ADEME 2020 (France): breakfast = 30% of per-night hotel footprint; 5-star 17.11 vs average 9.91 kgCO2e/night
Poore & Nemecek 2018 (OWID dataset): beef herd 99.5, dairy-herd beef 33.3, lamb 39.7, cheese 23.9, pork 12.3, poultry 9.9, eggs 4.7, vegetables ~0.5 kgCO2e/kg
Clune, Crossin & Verghese 2017 medians: beef 28.7, lamb 27.9, cheese 8.9, pork 5.9, chicken 4.1, eggs 3.4, milk 1.4, field vegetables 0.47 kgCO2e/kg
Scarborough et al. 2014 (UK): high meat-eaters 7.19 vs vegans 2.89 kgCO2e per 2,000 kcal day
WRI Cool Food Meals thresholds (US 2020): 3.59 kgCO2e/portion breakfast, 5.38 lunch/dinner; pledge -25% absolute or -38% per kcal by 2030
Mudie et al. 2016 (UK pub-restaurant kitchens): 1.52-3.32 kWh electricity per meal; 294 kWh/day/kitchen; refrigeration 41%, catering 63% of premises electricity

Kitchen energy benchmarks: ENERGY STAR 2014 restaurant split food prep 35/HVAC 28/sanitation 18/lighting 13/refrigeration 6%; audits 0.38-0.58 kWh elec per main meal (cooking only) and 1.28 kWh elec + 1.67 kWh gas per meal (institutional)
EPA Ireland hotel benchmarks: ~360 g food waste per cover (daily service), ~530 g per cover (functions), 263 g (restaurants); buffet breakfast 300 g vs plated 130 g per customer (unsourced)
Papargyropoulou et al. 2019 (Malaysia): 0.53 kg food waste per customer avg; 5-star hotel restaurant 8x a canteen; buffets most wasteful; banquet hall prepares 30% extra by policy
Camilleri-Fenech et al. 2020 (Malta 5-star): plate waste buffet dinner 0.48 vs a la carte dinner 0.16 / lunch 0.21 kg per person; prep waste 0.08 kg/person
Juvan et al. 2021 (Slovenia): breakfast-buffet plate waste 1.8 g (7-8am) -> 31.8 g (9-10am), avg 14.3 g/person; 4-star 14.3 vs budget 9.2 g; dinner late sitting 71-114 g vs early 27-32 g
Champions 12.3 / WRI / WRAP 2018: 42 hotel sites, 15 countries; -21% food waste by weight in 12 months; benefit-cost ratio avg 6.8:1, median 4.7:1; waste ~5% of COGS
Food-waste emission factors: DEFRA ~627 kgCO2e/t landfill vs ~9 kgCO2e/t composting; cradle-to-grave 1.9 kgCO2e/kg (BIO Intelligence 2010); WARM v16 compost-vs-landfill net 0.61 MTCO2e/short ton

Beverage LCAs: beer 510-842 gCO2e/L by packaging (Amienyo & Azapagic 2016, UK); wine 0.9-2.0 kgCO2e per 0.75 L bottle; single malt Scotch 2.83 kgCO2e per 70 cl (2025); gin 0.57 kg/70 cl; cocktails 152-690 g/drink (marketing)
Bar/kitchen equipment energy (ENERGY STAR certified): ice machines 3.6-5.6 kWh per 100 lb (~0.08-0.12 kWh/kg); high-temp door dishwashers 0.17-0.61 kWh per rack plus 0.45-1.0 kW idle
Minibars: Dometic HiPro absorption units 0.53-0.70 kWh/24h (236-265 kWh/yr, EN 62552-3); compressor ~1/3 of absorption (Tefcold claim); catalogue range 55-292 kWh/yr; ~70% of travellers never use one

Events: Dolder 7.8-8 kgCO2e per event guest (2023-24), 19.7 kg (2025); MeetGreen ~1.9 kg waste per attendee-day; GBTA 2023 532 kgCO2e/attendee (travel 42%); Hilton Cardiff 8 kgCO2 per person per full day of meals
Greek 5-star resort (CEST 2025): energy 81%, food waste 11%, other waste 5%, kitchen propane 3% of guest-night CO2e - operational boundary only, excludes purchased food

Gössling, Garrod, Aall, Hille & Peeters 2011 "carbon foodprint": review of food GHG intensity for tourism foodservice; abstract contains no kg CO2 per meal figure and notes "a lack of dependable data on the GHG intensity of foodstuffs"

Pirani & Arafat 2014 (hospitality solid-waste review) and 2016 (UAE food waste, 45 hotels/restaurants, FRESH indicator): bibliography and abstracts verified; neither abstract gives kg waste per room-night

Point, Tyedmers & Naugler 2012 (Nova Scotia wine LCA, functional unit one 750 mL bottle): viticulture and consumer transport dominate impacts; lighter bottles beat organic viticulture; third author is Naugler C, not "Theodore C"; abstract gives no kg CO2e per bottle
Option A: derive F&B share from a hotel-level Scope 3 inventory (Dolder 48-56%) rather than group disclosure (Accor 19%) or top-down sector split (SHA 62/19/17/2)
Option B1: count wasted food's embodied CO2e inside purchased-food Scope 3 and apply a disposal-only factor (DEFRA ~627 kgCO2e/t landfill, ~9 kg/t compost) to the waste line
Option B2: net purchases of wasted food and apply a cradle-to-grave waste factor (1.9 kgCO2e/kg BIO Intelligence 2010; Winnow-implied ~4.35 kgCO2e/kg) to the waste line
Option C: estimate kitchen/bar energy per cover bottom-up from measured kWh/meal (Mudie 1.5-3.3 kWh elec + ~1.7 kWh gas) vs top-down as 15-25% of whole-hotel energy (SHA, interview-based)
Carry embodied emissions of wasted food in the purchases bucket and use disposal-only waste factors (beats cradle-to-grave waste factor, which double counts with Scope 3 purchases)

nodes.t: Facet 3 established: F&B = 48-56% of a luxury urban hotel's CO2e (Dolder, full Scope 3) vs 19% at group level (Accor); 5-6 kgCO2e per restaurant cover; 1.5-3.3 kWh elec per meal; 0.3-0.5 kg waste per cover; beverages 0.15-0.33 kgCO2e per serve. Not found: hotel-kitchen kWh/cover, WRAP UK per-cover benchmark, Point 2012 bottle value, Filimonau 2011 breakfast figure, in-room coffee, glasswasher energy

facets.name: Guestrooms & services
facets.title: Facet 4: Guestroom and guest services footprint (HVAC, hot water, housekeeping/laundry, amenities, elevators, transport, behaviour levers)

nodes.t: PNNL 2010 sub-metered hotel: guestroom PTHP 4,016 kWh/day vs lights/TV 193 and minibar fridge 196 kWh/day (~300 rooms); DHW = 51% of gas; elevators 141 kWh/day (~1% of electricity)
CBECS 2018 lodging: 85.7 kBtu/ft2 total; water heating largest end use at 16.5 kBtu/ft2 (~20%); space heating ~20%; lighting, cooling each <=10%
HES/UNWTO 2011 European meta-analysis: hotels 200-400 kWh/m2/yr (avg 305-330); space conditioning ~50%, DHW up to 15%, lighting 12-18% (to 40%); no significant EUI difference by star rating
DOE/PNNL 2012 Marriott demo: occupancy-based guestroom HVAC controls saved 10.8-26.5% (mean 18.4%), 167-589 kWh/room/yr, payback 5.3-17.9 yr; prior utility studies 5.6-28% (62-462 kWh/room/yr)

Goldstein, Cialdini & Griskevicius 2008: descriptive-norm towel card raised reuse from 35.1% to 44.1% (same-room norm 49.3%); German replication (Bohner & Schlüter 2014) baseline 64.3%, messages 69-93%
Sheraton Boston opt-out housekeeping night saves 37.2 gal water, 0.19 kWh electricity, 25,000 BTU gas, 7 oz cleaning products; Hyatt Centric optional linen change cut linen output 18%
EPA WaterSense: washer-extractors 17-33 L/kg, tunnel washers <=17 L/kg; heating water = 0.048 kWh/L for a 41.7 K rise (before heater efficiency); water heating ~90% of washer energy

Hotel water per guest-night: 140 L European frontrunner benchmark (Styles 2015); 419 L weighted average across 1,667 hotels (Schick & Redlein 2025); 5-star 594 L vs 394 L average (Ecologic 2007/Hamele 2006); Marriott managed 788 L/occupied room (2022)

CHSB 2023 (2021 data, 25,576 hotels): luxury energy screened at 50-700 kWh/occupied room vs midscale 20-300; 5-star water per occupied room +23.3% 2019-21 vs 2-star +4.0%; luxury uses more water per room but not per m2
Gleick & Cooley 2009: bottled water 5.6-10.2 MJ per litre (1.6-2.8 kWh/L), dominated by PET bottle manufacture for short-haul water

No independent LCA of miniature toiletries vs bulk dispensers exists in accessible literature; chain claims are plastic-mass only (1 pump bottle = 10-12 minis; '95% less plastic'; Groupe GM '600 tCO2e')
DEFRA 2024 cars by market segment (kgCO2e/km): Luxury petrol 0.319, diesel 0.207, hybrid 0.258, PHEV 0.121; Executive petrol 0.208, diesel 0.170, hybrid 0.179, PHEV 0.086; BEV tailpipe 0

Hotel groups report no guest-travel Scope 3 category: Marriott 2022 lists purchased goods 4.13 Mt, capital goods 0.78, fuel/energy 1.65, waste 0.16, business travel 0.055, commuting 0.59, franchises 4.61 MtCO2e; Hilton franchises + waste + business travel; IHG SBT = Category 14

Elevators: ~1% of hotel electricity measured (PNNL 141 kWh/day, 12 storeys); 2-8% literature range for offices (Sachs 2005); hotels = ISO 'medium' usage ~300 trips/day; 22-135 Wh per empty reference cycle, 50-900 W standby
Bathroom lights left on 24 h = ~600 kWh/room/yr (4 x 60 W); motion-sensor control saves ~50% of bathroom lighting, 76-154 kWh/room/yr (PG&E ET 0609)

Deyà Tortella & Tirado 2011 (Mallorca hotel water): hierarchical regression of hotel water use; higher-category, low-season and all-inclusive models raise water consumption; management system and saving initiatives significant - abstract gives no L per guest-night

Gössling et al. 2012 (Tourism and water use review): direct tourism water use "considerably less than 1% of global consumption"; indirect use (food, materials, energy) likely larger than direct; no per-guest-night figure in abstract

facets.name: Targets & offsets
facets.title: Facet 5: Corporate climate targets (Hilton Travel with Purpose, SBTi) and offset / green-package strategies and their integrity

nodes.t: Hilton SBTi targets: -75% Scope 1+2 intensity (managed) and -56% Scope 3 intensity (franchised) by 2030 vs 2008, MT CO2e/m2; validated June 2022 as 1.5C-aligned

Hilton 2025 Performance Tables (DEKRA-assured): -50.9% managed / -36.0% franchised intensity vs 2008, but absolute market-based Scope 1+2 2,443,342 tCO2e (+9.6% vs 2008's 2,229,587) and franchise Scope 3 4,011,353 (+84% vs 2008's 2,180,912); location-based minus market-based Scope 2 gap 118,530 tCO2e = effect of green tariffs/EACs

Hilton LightStay: mandatory brand-standard monthly utility data from 7,500+ hotels; DEKRA limited assurance (ISO 14064-3, 5% materiality); progress tracked on market-based Scope 2; no credits in inventory
Marriott SBTi (Apr 2024): absolute -46.2% Scope 1+2 and -27.5% Scope 3 by 2030 vs 2019; net zero 2050 (-90%); yet 2.92% of energy from renewables (2023)
Peer targets: Hyatt -27.5% Scope 1+2 by 2030 vs 2019 (SBTi 2021); Accor -46% Scope 1+2 vs 2019, net zero 2050; IHG -15% absolute/-46% per m2 franchise (submitted); Minor/NH validated net zero 2050

Luxury independents: Six Senses -46% CO2 per occupied room by 2030 vs 2019; Iberostar 'carbon neutral' Scopes 1-3 by 2030 relying on nature offsets (SBTi-validated Oct 2022 but not 1.5C); Soneva 2% levy since 2008; Scandic neutrality-by-2025 goal (outcome unknown)

SBTi CNZS V1.3.1 (Apr 2026, valid through 2026): carbon credits 'do not count as reductions toward meeting near-term or long-term science-based targets'; only neutralise residuals at net zero or fund BVCM

SBTi CNZS V2.0 published 11 Jun 2026 (mandatory 31 Jan 2028): Ongoing Emissions Responsibility 1%/10%/100% at $20-80/t; removals mandatory from 2035 (1% rising to 100%); long-lived residuals need long-lived removals

SBTi V2.0 Scope 2 rules: PPAs/RECs allowed only from plants <=15 yrs in same deliverability region; large loads must report hourly matching; recognition at 50% (to 2030), 75% (to 2035), 90% (from 2035)

Hilton renewable procurement 2025: 35% of EMEA managed hotels/offices on renewable contracts; US managed hotels ~152M kWh renewable (+88% YoY, ~2% of managed energy); Istanbul/Dubrovnik solar PPAs 8M+ kWh (70% of demand)
SBTi April 2024 EAC controversy: Board statement 9 Apr allowing EACs/credits for Scope 3 abatement; staff letter 11 Apr; Board 12 Apr: 'no changes have been made to SBTi current standards'

West et al. 2023 (Science 381:873-877, 24 Aug 2023): 18 REDD+ projects, only 6.1% of credits tied to additional reductions; 68% from projects with no significant deforestation reduction; Verra disputes

California/IFM forest offsets over-credited: Badgley et al. 2022 GCB 29.4% (30.0 Mt, 90% CI 20.5-38.6); Coffield et al. 2022 GCB 37 IFM projects 'generally not additional'; Haya et al. 2023 Frontiers protocols deviate from science

ICVCM 15 Nov 2024: CCP label for ART TREES v2.0, VCS VM0048 v1.0, VCS JNR v4.1 only; legacy Verra REDD+ methodologies (majority of REDD+ credits, ~25% of all 2023 retirements) excluded; VCMI Claims Code tiers Silver 20-60%, Gold 60-100%, Platinum >100%

Oxford Principles 2024 (Smith School, Feb 2024): 'most offsetting today is still not net zero aligned'; reach 100% removal credits by net-zero date; durable storage; 'carbon neutral' is a 'less rigorous, interim claim'

CDR prices 2024-2025: durable removals ~$180/t vs ~$35/t nature-based; DAC median offtake ~$650/t ($100-989); biochar $50-150/t; weighted CDR avg $490 (2023) -> $320 (2024); Microsoft 93.8% of Q2 2025 volume (15.48 Mt record quarter)

Hotel neutrality programmes documented: Radisson Carbon Neutral Meetings (late 2012, Carbon Footprint Ltd, free to planner; 30,300 t offset since 2019); Hilton Carbon Neutral Meetings (2012 SE Asia; now ClimeCo, >=10 rooms on peak); Hyatt 14 US hotels 2023; Bucuti & Tara CarbonNeutral certified 28 Aug 2018 (wind-farm credits)

Populus Denver 'first carbon positive hotel' (2024): 6,675 tCO2e embodied carbon claimed offset via certified credits + 70,000 trees; CPR/Forest Service found 80% of spruce seedlings dead after one year (vs 46% avg)

Green-hotel WTP evidence: Kang et al. 2012 IJHM luxury/mid-price guests more willing than economy; Nelson et al. 2021 PLOS ONE 72.7% willing but mean ~US$1.55/night; Kuminoff et al. 2010 hedonic premium $9-26/room; Damigos 2023 review ~5% premium

Revealed opt-in behaviour is weak: Expedia CEO (Fortune, 6 Oct 2023) travellers 'choose the cheaper [option] the overwhelming majority of the time'; 2025 systematic review: stated willingness high, actual engagement low; Expedia TerraPass opt-in since 2006 ($5.99/1,000 lb)

Menu carbon labels: Brunner et al. 2018 Ecol Econ +11.5% low-emission dishes, -4.8% red-labelled, -3.6% emissions; canteen trials 1.5-5.0% emission cuts (Lowrie & Lohmann 2025 BPP summary incl. Lohmann et al. 2022 JEEM); workplace trials null (Pechey 2022, 111,837 choices); Camilleri et al. 2018 NCC labels cut beef soup choice

EU Directive 2024/825 (in force 26 Mar 2024; applies 27 Sep 2026): per se ban on 'neutral/reduced/positive impact' claims based on offsetting outside the value chain, unsubstantiated generic claims, and non-certified sustainability labels; Green Claims Directive stalled since June 2025

Court rulings on offset-based neutrality: KLM (Amsterdam, 20 Mar 2024, 15/19 statements misleading); Eurowings (LG Koln Mar 2024 81 O 32/23; OLG Koln 13 Dec 2024 6 U 45/24; OLG Dusseldorf I-20 U 38/25); BGH 27 Jun 2024 I ZR 98/23 ('klimaneutral' must say reduce vs offset); Best Western Mannheim hotel stays (LG Berlin II)

Regulators on hotel labels/claims: Booking.com dropped 'Travel Sustainable' badge (500,000+ properties) from 25 Mar 2024 after Dutch ACM objection; UK CMA fines up to 10% global turnover from 6 Apr 2025, ASA banned 'Eco Hotel' ads 9 Sep 2026; US FTC Green Guides unrevised since 2012

NYC Local Law 97 (2019): hotel (R-1) limits 0.00987 tCO2e/sf (2024-29) and 0.00526 tCO2e/sf (2030-34); penalty $268/tCO2e over limit; offsets max 10% of limit (AHRF only, $268/t); RECs deductible without cap but only Zone J-deliverable, same-year, utility electricity

Physical decarbonisation precedents: Hotel Marcel New Haven (Tapestry by Hilton, May 2022) all-electric with >1,000 PV panels, LEED Platinum reported, Passive House status inconsistent; Hilton Garden Inn Brussels Airport 2025 geothermal + 600 PV, 100% renewable; Hilton Istanbul/Dubrovnik solar PPAs 70% of demand

nodes.t: Guideline: state functional unit, boundary tier, allocation key and factor basis on the same line as the number; the methodological envelope for one luxury night is about 4.5x (1.7-2.4x boundary, 1.8-1.9x denominator, 1.36x NYC electricity factor)

Guideline: never report one denominator alone; rankings flip between per room-night, per guest-night and per m2 (CHSB US luxury 2.3x upper-midscale per OCRM but 1.43x per m2; Puig 2-star at 30% occupancy out-emits 5-star at 50%)

Guideline: four boundary tiers T0 Scope 1+2, T1 HCMI (+outsourced laundry), T2 operational Scope 3 (+food, waste, consumables), T3 life cycle; typical uplifts +5-10% (T0-T1), +40-130% (T1-T2), +15-43% (T2-T3)

Guideline: a guest-facing per-stay figure must be at least T2 (food, laundry, waste included) or be labelled T1; the Berlin Best Western ruling struck a neutrality claim because laundry and waste were omitted

Worked example on NYC luxury defaults (375 keys, 76.4% occupancy, CHSB medians): HCMI rooms 23.5 vs activity-based rooms 15.4 kgCO2e per occupied room-night; whole hotel 2,950 t, 28.2 per OCRM; T2 about 40 (+43%); benchmark hotel implies 955 ft2 per key vs about 2,700 at the Waldorf

Guideline: three electricity factors, three jobs - eGRID NYCW 0.392 for benchmarking, LL97 0.289 (0.145 from 2030) for compliance, market-based only beside location-based for target tracking; each 100 kWh/OCRM of electricity is worth 10.3 kgCO2e between the first two

Guideline: from 2026-28 only Zone J-deliverable, same-year, solely-owned RECs on electricity count under both LL97 and SBTi V2.0 (plants up to 15 years old, same deliverability region, hourly matching 50/75/90%); nothing touches Scope 1 from a gas plant

Guideline: metering priority is kitchens with cover counts, laundry with linen scales, a 10% guestroom HVAC sample with outdoor temperature, pool/thermal suite with heat meters and bather counts, elevators, zoned DHW; the evidence base has one metered guestroom set, one pool, one spa, zero kitchens or saunas
Rule 1: Boundary choice moves a per-night footprint more than property choice; adding food, waste and laundry to Scope 1+2 raises a full-service room-night 70-130% (9-56 kgCO2e for the same hotels)

Rule 2: Purchased food and drink is the largest single category once counted, 40-58% of a full-service room-night, and the share rises as the grid gets cleaner (Dolder 48-56% on Zurich grid vs Accor group 19%)

Guideline red flags: occupancy-insensitive electricity (Arenhart r=0.20 n.s., -0.21 upscale), EUI-only reporting (Waldorf ENERGY STAR 100 while closed, 97 under construction; GFA restatements +27-71%), vendor savings claims (33-50% vs 18.4% controlled), factor-set changes mid-series (eGRID 81.4-92.8-73.8; Dolder event figure 2.5x on database change)

Guideline: a compliant per-stay disclosure carries seven items on one line (number + unit, tier, allocation method, factor basis and year, data quality, named reductions, contributions in a separate sentence without neutral/net zero/offset/compensate) - satisfies Directive 2024/825, BGH I ZR 98/23, DUH v Best Western and SBTi V2 at once
Rule 3: Energy-only luxury footprints cluster at 20-50 kgCO2e per occupied room-night in the US and Western Europe; Asia and the Gulf run 50-95

Guideline: pools and thermal suites are allocated per bather, not per m2 of water surface - 30 L make-up per bather = 0.66 kWh thermal; Nitter 6.7-35 kWh per bather; published per-m2 WS range 1,000-11,000 with the most-quoted 4,300/5,200 unsourced
Rule 4: The normalising denominator changes rankings; per room-night, per guest-night (about half, at 1.80-1.92 guests/room) and per m2 give different orderings
Rule 5: Luxury premium is 2.3-3.1x midscale per occupied room-night but only 1.4-1.5x per m2; about 60% of the per-room gap is floor area per occupied room, 40% intensity per m2
Rule 6: Occupancy inverts star-rating rankings in per-night metrics; a 2-star at 30% occupancy (23 kgCO2e) out-emits a 5-star at 50% (22), pooled occupancy r = 0.20 n.s. and -0.21 for upscale

Rule 7: Area-based apportionment (HCMI) gives every room-night the same footprint regardless of amenity use, removes only ~5% from rooms in NYC luxury (28.39 vs 27.02), and no large benchmarking regression carries an amenity term
Rule 8: Electricity factor choice moves a NYC hotel's energy-only footprint 36-50% (eGRID NYCW 0.392 vs LL97 0.289 vs LL97-2030 0.145 kgCO2e/kWh), more than any measured operational intervention

Rule 9: Per-m2 intensity targets can be met while absolute emissions rise; chains reporting 11-51% intensity cuts show absolute emissions flat or up 8-84% (Hilton -50.9% intensity, +9.6% managed absolute, +84% franchise)

Rule 10: Offset-based carbon-neutral stay claims have failed scientifically (6.1% of REDD+ credits additional; 29.4% over-crediting in California forests) and legally (KLM, Eurowings, BGH, Best Western Berlin; EU 2024/825 per se ban from 27 Sep 2026), and the one hotel ruling turned on omitted laundry and waste
Rule 11: Water heating is the largest single end use in US lodging at ~20% of site energy (16.5 kBtu/ft2 in 2018, 24.2 in 2012) and 51% of a full-service hotel's gas; only HVAC as a whole exceeds it

Rule 12: Among wellness amenities only heated water (pools, hydrotherapy, thermal suites) carries a load of the order of guestroom HVAC and DHW (hotel pool-area heating 400-657 kWh/day vs DHW 299-1,574); treatment rooms and gyms add well under 1 kgCO2e per room-night

Rule 13: Pool energy scales with bathers and water throughput (bathers + opening days explain 77%), climate is secondary, and evaporation is 46-60%+ of pool-water heat loss; allocate by visits or m2 of water, not degree-days or floor area

Rule 14: A beef-centred main carries 8-11x a vegetarian main; a luxury-hotel restaurant cover runs 5.4-6.6 kgCO2e, about 3x a global-average meal and above the WRI Cool Food lunch/dinner threshold of 5.38
Rule 15: Hotel food waste runs 0.3-0.5 kg per cover with buffets 2-3x a la carte (Malta 0.48 vs 0.16-0.21 kg), and kitchens that weigh it cut it ~21% within a year at a 6.8:1 benefit-cost ratio

Rule 16: Linen laundry adds ~6-10 kWh and ~2-3 kgCO2e per occupied room-night at a full-service hotel (5-7 kg linen x 1.6-1.7 kWh/kg x 0.41 kgCO2/kg), corroborated by Sheraton Boston's 7.3 kWh gas + 0.19 kWh per opted-out night
I1: The F&B share of a hotel footprint is a property of the grid, not the hotel: 48-56% in Zurich, 19% at Accor group level, and it rises mechanically in NYC when the LL97 coefficient halves in 2030

Rule 17: Guest-behaviour and room-control levers each save at most 1-2 kgCO2e per occupied room-night (<10% of an energy-only luxury night); signage is cheap, hardware is not (5.3-17.9 yr paybacks), and 33-50% vendor claims fail controlled measurement
I2: Boundary moves the luxury room-night more than segment does: full-scope is 1.7-2.4x energy-only while luxury is 2.3x upper-midscale
I3: Denominator reverses the luxury verdict: 2.55x upper-midscale per room-night, 1.43x per m2; ~60% of the premium is area per key, and the Waldorf is at roughly 2,700 ft2 per key

Rule 18: Luxury hotels use 500-800 L water per occupied room-night (Marriott 788, Ecologic 5-star 594, Puig 580), 2-5x the 140 L frontrunner; the premium holds per room not per m2, and one 1,667-hotel review finds no quality effect

I4: The single-lot filing makes LL97 cap and hotel-only GFA two unknowns with one equation; the Studio's logged defaults imply a hotel area (~364,000 ft2, ~86% occupancy) 2.7x smaller than the report's bounding case (~1.0M ft2, 76.4%)

Rule 19: The operating phase is 70-90% of a hotel's life-cycle energy and emissions (Rossello-Batle 2010 70-80%); a 10-20% uplift on operational figures bounds embodied and amenity-production carbon for an existing building
I5: The 2030 LL97 cliff is a 61% cap cut against a 50% electricity-coefficient cut and 0% for gas; an all-electric Waldorf at the luxury peer EUI (135 kBtu/ft2) still exceeds the 2030 cap by ~49%
I6: Gas heat loses to any heat pump with COP above 1.95 on eGRID, 1.44 on LL97 2024-29 and 0.72 on LL97 2030, so "wait for the grid" has no carbon case in NYC

Rule 20: Dry in-room and building services (minibar 0.1-0.3 kgCO2e, elevator ~0.5 kWh, ice, dishwashing, toiletries, bottled water) each add under 1 kgCO2e per room-night, but one chauffeured 40 km airport transfer (8-13 kgCO2e one way) can exceed the room's Scope 1+2 night and no hotel group reports it
I7: After 2030 a gas CHP cannot beat the LL97 grid coefficient on electricity alone (would need 125% electrical efficiency; 63% even today); its case rests entirely on recovered heat

I8: Hilton's validated target is absolute (-46.2% S1+2 vs 2019); managed absolute S1+2 rose 2.23 to 2.44 Mt (2008-2025), the 2019 base is undisclosed, and Hilton's 2030 intensity goal (~39 kg/m2) converges on the LL97 2030 cap (~41 kg/m2), both a third of the Manhattan peer median (~122)

I9: Pool energy is driven by visitors and water, not climate (Kampel 2016; bather load R2 0.77), while every hotel benchmark normalises by climate; the Waldorf's only pool is residents-only, so it is in the LL97 denominator but not the guest-night numerator

I10: The Waldorf's wellness load is thermal suites with no measured data anywhere; at CIBSE TM46 fitness intensities the 22,000 ft2 spa is ~257 t/yr, ~2.5 kgCO2e per room-night (9% of the NYC luxury median) if charged to rooms rather than to $75 day-pass visits

I11: Claims law closes the offset route on 27 Sep 2026; the demand-side levers that remain legal move the footprint by 1.5-5% (menu labels) to 18.4% of guestroom HVAC (OBC), while the material levers (procurement, electrification, area per key) are invisible to guests

I12: The largest lines in a legally complete per-stay footprint are the ones no hotel group measures: a return luxury-car airport transfer (~25.6 kgCO2e) is 90% of the NYC luxury energy-only room-night (28.4)
I13: Cradle-to-grave food-waste factors (1.9-4.35 kg/kg) overstate the waste line 3-7x against disposal-only (0.627), and a 21% waste cut is ~4% of food carbon, not 21%

H2: Gas-side demand measures keep their carbon value through 2040 while electric-side measures lose half in 2030; sequence DHW, laundry and kitchen hot water before guestroom HVAC controls

H4: Procurement before kitchen: halving the meat share of food carbon beats full kitchen electrification on the full-scope guest-night in every year and has zero effect on LL97 exposure
H5: Retire the CHP in 2030; keeping the 555 kW CHP running after 2030 raises LL97 emissions versus grid purchase unless heat utilisation exceeds a computable threshold
H6: The full-scope multiplier on the Waldorf's energy-only night is below the Irish 1.7-2.4 under the 2024-29 LL97 factor and rises toward it under the 2030 factor with no change in the food knobs
H7: The Waldorf exceeds the CHSB NYC luxury upper quartile (38.19) per room-night at any hotel GFA per key above ~950 ft2 while sitting at the Manhattan peer median per m2
H8: Splitting the single-lot LL84 filing into hotel and multifamily raises the hotel's LL97 penalty exposure and lowers the residences', because the hotel floors are more intense per ft2

H9: Per guest-night the Waldorf's full-scope figure is less sensitive to the guests-per-room ratio than the energy-only figure, and the Studio's implied 1.6 is below the measured full-service 1.80-1.92
H10: Breakfast included in the rate adds 8-32% to an energy-only guest-night depending on the grid, and ADEME's 30% is the low-carbon-grid limit

H11: No single lever reaches the Waldorf's 2030 LL97 cap; only electrified heat plus ~30% demand cut from the luxury peer EUI plus Zone J RECs is compliant in 2030-34, and that story fails the 2035 cap without further measures
H12: The Waldorf's first LL84 operating year (CY2026) will read 15-40% worse per room-night than steady state because of occupancy ramp, while the per-m2 figure reads close to steady state
H13: Monte Carlo variance of the full-scope guest-night is dominated by the food factor set (beef 16.0 / 28.73 / 99.48 kg/kg), not by any amenity assumption
H14: The grid-factor choice (eGRID 0.392 vs LL97 0.289) changes the Scope 2 line by 36% and moves the F&B share more than any amenity knob at its full range
H15 (unsettleable): Hotel-only floor area and the hotel/residence energy split determine both the per-room-night result and LL97 exposure, and no public record will supply them

H16 (unsettleable): The Guerlain thermal suite's actual energy (infrared sauna, steam, hammam, snow cave, cryotherapy) is unknown within a factor of 3 and the simulator can only propagate the assumed range
